# Keeping and exchanging a song {#sec-files}

A native song and a MIDI file serve different purposes. The native file keeps
Modal's working structure and settings. A Standard MIDI File exchanges events
with other software. Choosing the right one avoids mistaking a useful
interchange copy for a complete working document.

## Native files keep the arrangement

The `.modal` format stores sections, track settings, local meters and the
musical events in plain text. A track's drum-map names are embedded too,
so moving the song preserves them without a separate map file. Positions within the file belong to sections,
so moving a section need not rewrite every event's position in the document.
The file can be inspected or kept in version control, but editing it by hand
is not required for normal work.

`:w` saves the current native song. A new song opens Modal's file picker; `:w FILE`
saves to a named file. With no extension Modal adds `.modal`. `:wq` saves
and quits. Native saves use a temporary file and replacement to avoid leaving
a partially written song if writing fails.

Unsaved changes are a property of the current song. Opening another song,
starting a new one or quitting refuses to discard them unless the corresponding
forced command is used. Closing the window offers the save decision. During
recording, the take must be stopped and finalised first, even for forced
commands.

Modal currently edits one song at a time: opening or creating another song
replaces the current one, subject to the unsaved-change checks above. There
are no song tabs or multiple open-song buffers in this version.

The native `.modal` file format is still under development. Compatibility
between files written by different development versions is not yet guaranteed.
Keep separate copies of important work before trying a newer build.
Undo history is a working-session facility, not a substitute for saved copies.

## Choosing a file {#sec-file-picker}

The picker lets you see the directory as you type or browse. `:e` opens it
beside the current song, or in your home directory for a new song. `:w` and
`:wq` use it when the song needs a filename. Drum-map commands without a
filename start in the reusable maps directory. `:write-config` starts in
the configuration directory and suggests `modalrc`.

Use Up and Down to choose a row and Enter to open it. A folder leads to its
contents, and `../` goes up to the parent. Alt-Down opens **Places**, where
you can jump to **Song**, **Config**, **Drum maps** or **State**. For example,
**State** is useful when opening a recovered song. Escape backs out of Places
or cancels the picker.

Typing narrows the list. Tab completes the common part of matching names
and then cycles through the choices. Completed folders end in `/` so you
can keep completing inside them. You can also type an absolute path, or a
path relative to the folder shown.

When saving, Enter on an empty filename accepts the suggestion. Type another
name to save elsewhere. If a file already exists, Modal asks before replacing
it. Press `n` or Escape to return to the picker and choose a different name.

## Importing MIDI

`:e FILE.mid` imports a Standard MIDI File, as does passing it to Modal at
startup. Import produces a Modal song that can then be saved natively.
A subsequent MIDI export is an interchange operation, not an instruction
to replace the native working copy.

A Modal track uses one output channel. MIDI material with multiple channels
is separated as needed on import, so its parts can have independent settings.
The conductor holds tempo and meter, while imported labels can describe
places in the song. `:label-to-section` (`, s l`) can turn those places into an
editable section structure once their meaning is understood.

Imported data is retained honestly, including unusual timing and overlapping
notes. An edit may refuse a new collision even though imported overlaps
already exist: preserving supplied data and creating more of it are separate
responsibilities.

## Exporting MIDI

`:export FILE.mid` writes a Standard MIDI File; with no filename it opens a
chooser. Export uses the stored events and their channels. Playback-only
transpose, velocity, timing and quantise settings are not all baked into it,
and mute or solo does not select a subset for export. Freeze a chosen
playback result first when the destination should receive those changes.

Track bank and program setup is an exception: it is written at the start
so that the receiving program can choose the requested sound. Reimporting
that file reads those setup messages as events, because MIDI does not mark
them as Modal-specific track settings.

The conductor's meter becomes the MIDI file's shared time signature. Independent
track meters, section editing structure, machine routing and Modal's working
state cannot all be represented by that shared interchange model. A `.mid`
export should therefore accompany, rather than replace, the native song
when those distinctions matter.

An existing named output file is protected from accidental overwrite.
The bang follows the command, as in `:export! FILE.mid` or `:w! FILE`.
It does not go at the end of the path. A chooser may supply its own overwrite
confirmation.

Each command keeps to its own kind of file, because a file is read back by
its name: `:w` refuses a name ending `.mid` or `.midi`, and `:export` one
ending `.modal`, each saying which command writes that kind.

## File-command summary

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `:e` / `:e FILE` | Choose or name a song or MIDI file to open |
| `:new` | Start a new song |
| `:w` / `:w FILE` | Save the native song, or save to a chosen path |
| `:export` / `:export FILE.mid` | Write a MIDI interchange copy |
| `:q` | Quit, protecting unsaved changes |
| `:wq` | Save and quit |
| `:source` | Re-read application configuration; it does not open a song |
| `:write-config` | Write application preferences; it does not save the song |
| `:drum-map-load [FILE]` | Load a drum map into the current track, or choose a file |
| `:drum-map-save[!] [FILE]` | Save a reusable map; `!` reviews an existing copy before replacing it |

Relative song paths start in the song's folder, or the home folder for an
unsaved song. Configuration commands use the configuration directory instead;
drum-map files start in its `drum-maps/` subdirectory. See @sec-drum-maps for
map ownership and comparison.
Completion shows the base directory when offering filenames. A path beginning
with `~` starts at the home directory.

## When the result is unexpected

The most useful first evidence is the message row. A refused operation leaves
a reason there: an overlap, an unavailable port, an invalid value or a recording
track that cannot be edited yet. Repeating the same keys without considering
the reason will usually repeat the same refusal.

If notes appear in the right place but sound different, inspect track playback
settings and the receiving instrument's program and controllers. If a MIDI
export sounds different in another program, check which playback transforms
still need freezing and how that program chooses its instruments. If input
activity is visible but silent, distinguish input reception, arming, Thru,
output routing and the receiver's audio path.

For a reproducible problem, keep a small song that demonstrates it, the exact
commands or keys, the operating system and the relevant MIDI route. The
state directory's `crash.log`, if present, records unexpected application
errors with a version and time. This is more useful than assuming that every
silence or warning is a timing problem.

If Modal ever does stop on such an error while a song has unsaved changes, it
saves the song as it was into the state directory, named `recovered-` and the
time, and says where when it next starts. Open that file with `:e`, save it
under the name it should have with `:w FILE`, then delete the recovered copy.
It is a last resort rather than a substitute for saving.

## Companion command-line tools

`modal-ports` lists visible inputs and outputs. `modal-play` and `modal-record`
provide terminal-based MIDI playback and recording with their own `--help`.
They are separate programs, not commands for Modal's colon prompt.

`modal-loopback` measures timing through a real MIDI route. Its results depend
on the interface, driver and test setup. Software tests and offscreen figures
do not measure those hardware properties. The repository's `docs/tools.md`
contains the detailed diagnostic options; most musical work should begin
with the GUI's port and track information instead.
